items._ogDesc: A new report says Ontario’s housing market is expected to improve “modestly” next year as favourable economic conditions help push buyers off the sidelines.
items.body:
TORONTO — A new report says Ontario’s housing market is expected to improve “modestly” next year as favourable economic conditions help push buyers off the sidelines, though higher borrowing costs could dull the extent of the rebound.

Desjardins senior economist Kari Norman calls the province’s housing sector “weak” despite improved affordability, greater buyer choice and easing rental conditions.

Her report predicts existing home sales would rise nearly five per cent in 2027 compared with this year, remaining well below long‑term norms, while balanced market conditions should lead to average price growth of 2.4 per cent next year.

  • Most recent real estate news from BNNBloomberg.ca

The analysis also says the interest rate backdrop will “likely remaining challenging,” with two rate hikes by the Bank of Canada expected in 2027 that would limit affordability gains from recent home price declines and rising disposable incomes.

That would also raise construction financing costs, as the report projects housing starts to rise around six per cent to nearly 65,000 units in 2027 — still more than 30 per cent below levels seen in 2021 and 2022.

The report says rental conditions should remain relatively balanced, as new condominium and purpose‑built rental completions add supply at a time when population growth is likely to be weak.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

items.title: WSIB job cuts causing a ‘crisis,’ union says
items.description: The union representing Workplace Safety and Insurance Board employees says services have been negatively impacted since job cuts and local centres were closed two months ago.

items._ogDesc: The union representing Workplace Safety and Insurance Board employees says services have been negatively impacted since job cuts and local centres were closed two months ago.
items.body:
The union representing Workplace Safety and Insurance Board employees says services have been negatively impacted since the announcement of job cuts and local centres were being closed two months ago.

Ten WSIB locations across the province were closed and hundreds of jobs were cut, half in northern Ontario.

“Injured workers and their representatives report waiting two to three hours on the phone lines,” said Harry Goslin, president of the Ontario Compensation Employees Union at a news conference at Queen’s Park on Tuesday.

“Unassigned claims have increased 15-fold, leaving thousands of workers without support.”

He said since the locations closed and more than 500 positions eliminated, Goslin said the remaining workers have heavier workloads. That is having an impact on services for those who’ve filed claims with the WSIB.

“How can WSIB staff support injured workers when they themselves are working in a toxic and unsafe environment?” he said.

“The WSIB is in a crisis and is now offering overtime. You don’t cut hundreds of jobs and then offer overtime unless the work is still there … It is a direct acknowledgement that the WSIB no longer has enough staff to meet the service demands.”

“Despite promises by the WSIB that there’d be no impact to service, front-line staff report call times have increased from three to 20 minutes to as long as two to three hours,” said Sudbury NDP MPP Jamie West.

The Toronto news conference was organized by West and Lise Vaugeois, MPP for Thunder Bay-Superior North.

Vaugeois is the NDP critic for WSIB and Workers with Disabilities, while West is the NDP critic for Labour.

Both said the restructuring has had a major impact on northern Ontario since half the closed sites were in the region and all regional positions were eliminated.

“If all of those people are in southern Ontario -- and that’s assuming that they’re people and not AI chatbots -- they don’t know those circumstances,” Vaugeois said, referring to regional and industry expertise.

“We’ve heard stories of (WSIB workers in southern Ontario asking) ‘why don’t you just take a Go-Train?’ That, of course, is an absurd remark for anybody who lives in the north; such a thing doesn’t exist.”

Vaugeois said it’s important for WSIB workers “to understand those conditions,” such as the type of work, weather and roadways northern Ontarians deal with regularly.

The NDP has asked Ontario’s Auditor General to audit the WSIB’s restructuring and whether the decision was supported by “sound governance, effective government oversight, prudent financial management and adequate evidence.”

The WSIB is adamant there are still local teams providing in-person support in Sudbury and across northern Ontario, as well as both industry and injury experts on hand for assistance.

Aaron Lazarus, the WSIB’s vice-president of communications, told CTV News the restructuring was about providing value for Ontario businesses paying insurance premiums.

He said the WSIB helps “almost 9 of 10 people return to work within three months of that injury,” while at the same time reducing premiums for businesses by 50 per cent in the last 10 years.

  • Download the CTV News app now

“One person doesn’t have to lose in order for the other to win. We’re able to, as an organization, look at how we can help people return to work and be the most effective and efficient as possible to have the lowest premium rates as possible for Ontario businesses,” Lazarus said.

“We are doing great work -- we have an amazing team across Ontario, including in Sudbury, who are putting everything of themselves into helping people,” he said, adding “it’s a special place to work.”

“We hope you never need us, but if you do, because of an injury or illness, the WSIB is here to help.”

items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney says Ottawa will 'not budge' from its goal of making immigration intake numbers sustainable and the federal government is 'getting them to that level now.'
items.body:
OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney says Ottawa will “not budge” from its goal of making immigration intake numbers sustainable and the federal government is “getting them to that level now.”

Carney says he’s been in talks with the provinces about getting immigration “to the right levels” as well about how new Canadians can be most effectively distributed across the country and the economy.

His comments come after just over a million Albertans voted yes to a referendum question calling for more provincial control over immigration policy to reduce the number of newcomers to “sustainable levels.”

About 53 per cent of voters said ‘yes’ to that question.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Tuesday the Liberals have let immigration run “totally out of control” and provinces should have more control over immigration numbers because they have to deliver services for newcomers.

Immigration Minister Lena Diab did not respond to reporters’ questions when she walked into the weekly Liberal caucus meeting, but the federal immigration levels are due for an update by next month.

MONTREAL — The Public Sector Pension Investment Board has signed a deal to launch a joint venture with Nuveen Real Estate to invest in open-air shopping centres in the United States.

The partnership is starting with a US$790-million portfolio.

PSP Investments says the strategy is demographically driven, focusing on open-air shopping centres anchored by grocers, necessity-based retailers, and essential services.

  • Latest updates on investing here

It is targeting U.S. metro areas with strong population growth, rising household incomes and high barriers to entry, where retailers are seeking to expand.

To date, PSP Investments and Nuveen say they have closed deals on 19 assets in Virginia, Arizona, Florida, Minnesota, Texas, California, Colorado, and Washington.

PSP Investments invests money for the pension plans of the federal public service, the Canadian Forces, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and the Reserve Force.

items.title: Wall St says Tesla-SpaceX deal inevitable but Musk says it’s not certain
items.description: Elon Musk sees “a lot of merit” in combining Tesla and SpaceX, but the decision is not his to make. Tension runs through a deal that many analysts call inevitable.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Elon Musk attends the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, Jan. 22, 2026. (AP Photo/Markus Schreiber, File)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Markus Schreiber</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Elon Musk sees “a lot of merit” in combining Tesla and SpaceX, but the decision is not his to make. Tension runs through a deal that many analysts call inevitable.
items.body:
Elon Musk sees “a lot of merit” in combining Tesla and SpaceX, but the decision is not his to make: two special committees he cannot join and a Tesla shareholder vote he calls a high hurdle stand in the way.

That tension runs through a deal that many analysts call inevitable. Musk, a self-described ‘conflicted party’, said the committees are yet to agree on the terms and a merger is not certain, even though Wall Street expects a deal by the end of next year.

Tesla shares gained more than three per cent while SpaceX rose 12 per cent and were on track for their biggest percentage gain since early August.

  • Latest updates on company news here

SpaceX and Tesla are jointly developing the Terafab chip plant, and AI now makes up more than half of SpaceX’s revenue, with another US$35 billion to US$40 billion spending likely in fourth quarter to fund further expansion.

“I think a Tesla-SpaceX merger makes sense. It’s very strategic because both companies are rapidly transitioning into artificial intelligence and autonomous systems, and both have huge infrastructure projects underway,” said Justus Parmar, CEO of Fortuna Investments and an investor in both companies.

“It would also avoid redundancy and the time he spends going back and forth between two entities, and there would be a reduction in public company overhead, legal costs and administrative burdens.”

Analysts have said that burgeoning capital spending for expensive AI and space infrastructure would weigh on SpaceX’s free cash flow, a strain a combined company could ease by sharing services and borrowing jointly with Tesla.

They also pointed to last week’s Roadster unveiling, where a Tesla car built with SpaceX rocket thrusters flipped and leapt over vehicles, as a teaser for what a combined company could produce.

However, much of the technology on which the lofty valuations of the companies are based, including data centers in orbit, self-driving taxis at scale and humanoid robots, has yet to reach commercial scale.

That would take years of heavy spending and engineering, adding execution risk to a deal already facing questions over governance and price.

“The big reason why this makes so much sense is that what Tesla is doing SpaceX needs and what SpaceX is doing Tesla needs,” Gene Munster, managing partner at Tesla investor Deepwater Asset Management, said on X.

“And both of them operate under the grand vision which is Elon building a true vertical AI company.”

Tesla vote in the hurdle

Control may also be part of Musk’s appeal for a merger. Musk holds about 85 per cent of SpaceX’s voting power through super-voting shares. But at Tesla he has roughly 20 per cent.

Bill Birmingham, head of research at REX Financial, estimates a merger would give the billionaire about 57 per cent of voting rights.

Ryan Zurrer, founder of Dialectic, puts it at 58 per cent at an exchange ratio of 0.7 of one SpaceX share, the illustrative level Barclays has floated.

No ratio has been negotiated. Zurrer said a ratio near 0.6 would be needed for Musk to keep control if he sold more equity, and that “the biggest hurdle will be the Tesla shareholders vote vs Elon’s own incentives.”

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Musk said Tesla side needs a majority of all shares, not just those voted, so every uncast ballot counts against a deal. Analysts have flagged turnout as a risk, citing uncast broker votes at last year’s meeting as a potential factor that could affect chances of a deal going through.

Governance and regulatory questions would follow. When Tesla bought SolarCity in 2016, a Delaware court cleared it after years of litigation but said it should have formed an independent committee.

“A deal where one man runs both sides will draw tough questions on governance,” said Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for APAC at eToro.

Tesla is set to report third-quarter results after markets close. Analysts said they were also watching out for disclosures of merger talks in regulatory filings ahead of the automaker’s Dec. 3 annual shareholder meeting.

Reporting by Abhirup Roy in San Francisco and Akash Sriram in Bengaluru; Additional reporting by Arpan Daniel Varghese in Bengaluru; Editing by Arun Koyyur

items.title: End of an era? How the Hermes Birkin bag is losing its scarcity appeal
items.description: London-based Cai Baochun used to make a hefty profit reselling Hermes’ famed Birkin bags for more than double their US$10,000 retail price. Now he has stopped stockpiling them as second-hand prices fall.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A Bonhams employee displays a Hermes Rose Sakura Swift Leather Birkin 25 bag at the auction rooms in London, Monday, Feb. 26, 2024. (AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Kirsty Wigglesworth</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: London-based Cai Baochun used to make a hefty profit reselling Hermes’ famed Birkin bags for more than double their US$10,000 retail price. Now he has stopped stockpiling them as second-hand prices fall.
items.body:
PARIS/LONDON -- London-based Cai Baochun used to make a hefty profit reselling Hermes’ famed Birkin bags for more than double their US$10,000 retail price. Now he has stopped stockpiling them as second-hand prices fall.

“I don’t want to lose money,” said Cai, who started selling the bags on online platforms such as Vestiaire Collective and on social media in 2020 and rode a pandemic-era luxury spending boom.

The resale value of unworn Birkins sold as second-hand online has dropped by more than $6,000 from its 2022 peak, he said.

The decline reflects a broader shift in the market for one of luxury’s most exclusive products whose appeal and success have been driven by scarcity.

Increasing supply of Birkin bags in the second-hand market is depressing resale premiums, according to resellers, industry consultants and analysts interviewed by Reuters, raising questions about a strategy that helped propel Hermes to become one of the world’s most profitable luxury companies.

Named after the late British-French actor Jane Birkin, the handbag has been central to Hermes’ performance. Between 2015 and 2025, group annual sales tripled to €16 billion (US$18 billion) while its market value surged. Last year, Hermes posted an operating margin of 41 per cent, above that of rivals including Chanel, Kering-owned Gucci and LVMH’s leather and fashion division, which includes Louis Vuitton and Dior.

Resale market under pressure

All of that was underpinned by an aura of exclusivity.

Six resellers who source bags directly from Hermes shoppers said access to a Birkin is generally linked to spending on Hermes scarves, clothes and shoes, although the exact policy differs between regions and stores. Two estimated customers typically spend $10,000 to $20,000 before being offered the Birkin or the Kelly, the brand’s other popular bag.

Hermes, which says a Birkin takes 15 hours to craft, does not disclose its selling policies or how many bags it makes. It declined to comment for this story.

Of the nine Birkin resellers Reuters interviewed in the US, Europe and Asia, six said resale prices had fallen over the past year as more handbags became available, while five reported softer demand.

Antoinette Hunter, who founded luxury handbag reseller Lilac Blue in 2007, said when she got the first request for a Birkin, few people knew the bag. She eventually sourced one from a member of Japan’s royal family.

Acquiring Birkins is no longer a challenge, Hunter said, but it’s harder to make money from resales. She said the price for an unworn black Birkin 25 bag, one of the most sought-after models, has fallen by around £4,000 (US$5,336) since 2022, to around £24,000. Cai, who sells via Vestiaire Collective and Instagram, says his price for the bag is around £20,000.

Hermes sells the same model for £9,390 in Britain, a Hermes sales assistant in London said.

Although Hunter still sees plenty of demand for Hermès bags, particularly the most high-end ones, she said the decline in resale prices might dissuade some from buying directly from Hermes.

“If Hermes continues to raise the prices, and the prices on the resale market continue to drop, that margin gets squeezed, and perhaps it will become less appealing,” she said.

Brokerage Bernstein, which tracks individual auction results, said in a September note the resale price on Birkin 25 bags averaged about 1.7 times the retail tag in the third quarter, down from about 2.6 times at their 2022 peak.

Business model under scrutiny

Hermes’ leather goods division, which includes other handbag models, generates 44 per cent of annual group revenue.

For more than a decade, limited supply and strong demand allowed Birkins to command hefty resale premiums, benefiting both Hermes and resellers as the prospects of making a profit via the secondary market encouraged Hermes clients to buy more from the brand.

“It was a win-win,” said Sarah Davis, founder of California-based Fashionphile. The company said its Birkin listings have grown 32-fold in 15 years. The company’s website currently lists 212 Birkins on sale.

Hermes has gradually expanded the production of its handcrafted items, opening one workshop per year on average. Meanwhile, the rise of resale platforms such as Vestiaire Collective and The RealReal, alongside vintage boutiques with online shops and social media channels, has made it easier than ever to resell.

The bags and other Hermes items remain highly sought after, resellers said, but the brand is showing some strain.

Hermes’ shares have lost nearly 40 per cent of their market value this year, making the brand one of the worst performers among listed luxury companies.

Earlier this month, UBS analysts downgraded Hermes shares to “sell,” saying that growing secondary-market supply of Birkins and Kellys could weaken the brand’s scarcity-driven business model.

“We believe the nature of the business is changing,” they said in a note, estimating that the number of the handbags listed for sale worldwide is now six to seven times higher than before the pandemic.

The company is expected to report quarterly sales growth of 5.2 per cent on Thursday, which would mark its weakest quarterly growth in six years, according to Visible Alpha estimates.

While leather goods revenue is still expected to grow by 10 per cent, demand for clothing, silk scarves and perfumes is cooling, a sign fewer customers are making the purchases traditionally required to buy a Birkin at a later stage, two equities analysts and two industry consultants said.

Asked in July whether Hermes should slow production to protect the brand, Hermes CEO Axel Dumas told reporters that some people feared making too many bags would hurt its exclusivity, while others questioned why it was not making more.

He added that output depended largely on the number of fully trained artisans and available high-quality leather.

Not all resellers see weakness. Davis said prices for the bag on the Fashionphile platform have remained firm and even risen slightly this year, pointing to renewed attention generated by Norwegian soccer star Erling Haaland’s handbag collection.

Reporting by Tassilo Hummel, additional reporting by Helen Reid in London; Editing by Lisa Jucca and Emelia Sithole-Matarise, Reuters

items.title: ‘Alarm and concern’: Canada’s Armenian population reacts to PM’s trip to Türkiye
items.description: Mark Carney’s trip to Türkiye Wednesday marks the first ever bilateral visit to the country by a Canadian prime minister.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark Carney meets with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Ankara, Turkey, Tuesday, July 7, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu"></media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Mark Carney’s trip to Türkiye Wednesday marks the first ever bilateral visit to the country by a Canadian prime minister.
items.body:
Mark Carney’s trip to Türkiye Wednesday marks the first ever bilateral visit to the country by a Canadian prime minister.

Carney will sit down with Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Ankara Wednesday, before heading to Istanbul for a series of business meetings. His office is not releasing who else he plans to meet with ahead of the trip.

While Reuters reports Canada and Türkiye will sign a joint declaration aimed at deepening ties in four areas including defence and energy, senior officials repeatedly declined to say what announcements are expected, beyond that something would be announced.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Another government source suggested what’s in the works is not finalized enough to the point of being able to share.

Officials did say the areas of trade focus include defence, energy, mining, tech and agriculture.

University of Ottawa international affairs Prof. Thomas Juneau calls Türkiye a “competitive autocracy” – too far removed to be considered a democracy.

The former Middle East policy analyst for the Department of National Defence agrees with the Carney government calculus that diversifying trade away from the United States requires going beyond dealing with pure democracies.

“The challenge, if, on moral grounds, we decide to limit our diversification efforts to democracies, is that there’s just not that many of them,” Juneau said.

“If we are to be serious in really being successful in diversifying our partnerships, trade and security, we simply must go beyond the small number of democracies, and that includes countries like Saudi Arabia, like Türkiye, with whom we do have common interests, but with whom we also do have serious disagreements,” Juneau told CTV News.

“Canada certainly engages with countries where we do not share 100 per cent of the values in all ways,” said one senior official at the briefing.

In July, speaking in Saudi Arabia on the same G20 trip that saw him visit Ankara, Carney said he believes “lecturing countries from afar is an ineffective strategy.”

At the G20 summit, Canada and Türkiye announced they were formally launching talks towards a free trade agreement.

Deepening ties with Türkiye has faced criticism, especially from Canada’s large Armenian diaspora.

“As Canadians, we’re very supportive of the government’s efforts to diversify trade relations. We just do not believe at all that Türkiye is the right partner,” Sevag Belian of the Armenian National Committee of Canada told CTV News, specifically mentioning human rights concerns and the country’s “destabilizing role” in the region.

Belian says the community is reacting to the trip with “alarm and concern.”

He says the biggest worry is that as part of the deepening of ties, Canada may reverse its stance on recognition of the Armenian genocide. Canada officially recognized the Armenian Genocide in 2004.

“We are very fearful that the Turkish side will put this issue on the table. But we are hopeful that the Canadian side won’t budge,” Belian says.

The University of Waterloo’s Bessma Momani doesn’t think the issue will be reopened.

But she tells CTV News, for the cost benefit analysis of dealing with Türkiye to be worth it, the trip must amount to more than a series of photo-ops.

“The way to make this worth it is to actually sign some real deals, investment, have corporations, both Canadian corporations investing in Türkiye, and similarly Turkish companies investing here-that will be the proof of success,” Momani said.

This summer, the government ran consultations allowing Canadians to weigh in on a potential free trade deal with Türkiye. While the processed wrapped up Sept. 14, a summary of what they found has not yet been released, and officials at the briefing declined to share a sense of the findings.

The defence relationship has been rocky, with Canada suspending arms export permits in 2020. A government report found evidence the country was using Canadian military technology, specifically sensors used on Turkish drones, in the conflict in the Nagorno-Karabakh region of Azerbaijan.

That ban was lifted in 2024, with Canada now assessing exports on a case-by-case basis.

“We are in a position to resume a more regular export relationship, and we will continue to monitor,” a government official said.

Carney will be joined on the trip by Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson. Anand visited Türkiye in March, and hosted her counterpart in Canada in June.

Canada has faced criticism for not specifically condemning the ongoing crackdown in Türkiye on LGBTQ2S+ groups. Anand has said that shouldn’t be interpreted as a lack of solidarity with oppressed people.

Tuesday, senior government officials pointed to Canada signing on to this Equal Rights Coalition statement condemning the persecution of LGBTIQ+ activists globally as a violation of human rights. It doesn’t specifically mention Türkiye.

Hodgson’s presence underlines the significance of Canada’s energy sector to the burgeoning trade relationship, though government officials would not say whether any deal to purchase Canadian CANDU reactor or SMRs was in the cards for this trip.

Türkiye is “desperate for energy,” says Momani, pointing to its reliance on “not trustworthy” countries like Iran and Russia in the past.

“They would very much like to have Western, NATO members to procure as much energy as possible, whether it’s nuclear or LNG or any other clean tech, all of it is something that I think Türkiye is desperately in need of,” she said.

items.title: Wall Street drifts as SpaceX climbs and Netflix falls
items.description: U.S. stocks are ticking higher as strong profit reports from companies help offset updates from Netflix and AT&T that investors found disappointing.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Specialist Dilip Patel works on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, Thursday, July 30, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Yuki Iwamura</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: U.S. stocks are ticking higher as strong profit reports from companies help offset updates from Netflix and AT&T that investors found disappointing.
items.body:
NEW YORK — The U.S. stock market is drifting Wednesday as strong profit reports from SpaceX, Capital One Financial and other big companies work against updates from Netflix and AT&T that investors found disappointing.

The S&P 500 was virtually unchanged, coming off two straight modest gains. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 30 points, or 0.1 per cent, as of 10:15 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.4 per cent higher.

SpaceX helped lead the market and climbed 11.1 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Elon Musk, who runs the company that makes money from artificial-intelligence technology, rockets and other businesses, also said that SpaceX took a step to consider a possible merger with Tesla, his electric-vehicle company.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

Tesla, which will report its latest quarterly results late Wednesday, climbed 3.3 per cent and was one of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500.

Other stocks rallying on profit reports that topped analysts’ expectations included Capital One Financial, which rose 4.1 per cent, and Winnebago Industries, which climbed 7.2 per cent.

Expectations are high for profit growth during the summer, and companies will need to meet them to justify the big runs their stock prices have made toward records despite worries about high inflation, higher interest rates and other challenges weighing on Wall Street.

Winnebago was able to report a more resilient profit than analysts expected even as high fuel prices and frustration among U.S. shoppers restrain interest in recreational vehicles, for example. CEO Michael Happe said its more expensive towable RVs are a tougher sell, but customers are interested in its “more accessible” offerings.

On the losing side of Wall Street was Netflix, which fell 4.2 per cent even though the streaming service reported a stronger profit than analysts expected. Investors focused instead on worries that Netflix’s momentum may be slowing. The company’s forecast for revenue growth in the final three months of the year fell short of analysts’ expectations.

AT&T fell 5.6 per cent even though it likewise delivered a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for growth this year in an underlying measure of earnings before income taxes and some other things that fell short of some analysts’ expectations.

Among AI stocks, which have been at the center of the market’s action in recent weeks, the movements remained unsettled.

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

After leading the rest of the market for years because of the frenzy around AI, stocks in the industry have become shaky on worries that the build out of data centers may slow because of how much more expensive it’s become to borrow money.

CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly volatile. On Tuesday, it careened between a loss of 6 per cent and a gain of 5 per cent, for example. On Wednesday, it fell 2.1 per cent after erasing an early gain of nearly 4 per cent.

Other AI-linked stocks were more resilient. Nvidia’s gain of 0.9 per cent was the strongest force lifting the S&P 500.

Besides SpaceX’s profit report showing strength for AI spending, another encouraging signal for the industry came from Super Micro Computer, which sells AI servers and services. It said it expects to report stronger revenue for the summer than it had earlier forecast because of “increased demand for AI platforms,” and its stock rallied 11.4 per cent.

  • Latest updates on investing here

Another potential boost for the AI industry came from an easing of Treasury yields in the bond market, which helps dictate how expensive loans are for the U.S. government, companies and regular Americans.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.09 per cent from 5.12 per cent late Tuesday, though it remains far above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation higher.

Oil prices remained unsteady on Wednesday following big swings this month on uncertainty about when the energy industry can return to normal. The price for a barrel of Brent crude added 0.2 per cent to US$108.96 after swinging up and down through the morning. It’s been yo-yoing between US$97 and US$112 in October.

In stock markets abroad, indexes rose in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 3.3 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves as AI stocks regained strength.

items.title: Ottawa is selling homes fast – but building the wrong kind
items.description: A record sales run is raising questions about what gets built next in Ottawa
items.content: <p>A record sales run is raising questions about what gets built next in Ottawa</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639281937065157840.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A record sales run is raising questions about what gets built next in Ottawa
items.body:
Ottawa’s new home market posted its strongest September in recent memory, with 521 sales recorded. That's an 81.5% increase from the 287 transactions closed in September 2025, according to data from the Greater Ottawa Home Builders’ Association (GOHBA) and PMA Brethour Realty Group.

Month-over-month, activity climbed 12.3% from August’s 464 units. Year-to-date, 4,078 new homes have sold in Ottawa through September, up 53.8% from 2,652 at the same point last year.

Supply gap persists despite record sales pace

Housing starts in Ottawa are up 14% in 2026, with 8,169 homes under construction compared with 7,168 in the same period last year, according to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC).

However, the gains have not kept pace with demand for ownership housing. Much of that pipeline is weighted toward rental, raising the prospect that Ottawa’s affordability recovery could go into reverse if the ownership supply gap continues to widen.

Jason Burggraaf, Executive Director of the Greater Ottawa Home Builders’ Association in Ontario, said September’s gains carry an important caveat.

“September’s sales are encouraging, but CMHC’s latest report shows Ottawa still faces a widening housing supply gap, with much of its construction activity concentrated in rentals,” Burggraaf said.

“Improving affordability means supporting more ownership housing too. Finalizing the development charge reduction agreement is an immediate opportunity to lower building costs, and we’re pushing for a timely resolution so some 2026 construction can benefit.”

The concern echoes comments Burggraaf made on Ottawa’s August new home sales results, when he cautioned, “Governments need to ensure that the way we fund growth doesn’t add costs that put those homes further out of reach.”

Geographically, Ottawa’s west end captured 43% of September sales, with the south at 40%, together accounting for 83% of all transactions.

The east recorded 15% and Central Ottawa 2%. Townhomes led all product types at 44%, followed by single-detached homes at 35% and condo townhomes at 20%.

Development charge relief within reach

City council approved a plan in July to reduce development charges by 54% over three years, tied to a joint federal-Ontario infrastructure fund.

Under that framework, charges on single-family and semi-detached homes inside the Greenbelt would fall to $25,752, with suburban builds set at $28,781.

Development charges are one-time fees levied on new residential properties to fund growth-related capital infrastructure.

The push to finalise the agreement comes as Canada’s housing affordability reached a four-year best in Q1 2026, according to RBC Economics, with the national aggregate measure falling to 53% of pre-tax median household income required to cover ownership costs.

items.title: Canadian consumer confidence climbs, but housing optimism lags
items.description: Home price optimism trails as brokers brace for the Bank of Canada’s October 28 decision
items.content: <p>Home price optimism trails as brokers brace for the Bank of Canada’s October 28 decision</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639281927714349803.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Home price optimism trails as brokers brace for the Bank of Canada’s October 28 decision
items.body:
Canadian consumer confidence firmed in mid-October, yet Canadians’ outlook for home values, the measure that matters most to mortgage brokers, still sits well below its historical norm.

The Bloomberg Nanos Canadian Confidence Index (BNCCI) reached 51.68 for the four weeks ending October 16, up from 49.86 a month earlier.

The weekly gauge is compiled from a rolling telephone survey of 1,016 Canadians. It sits above the neutral 50 mark but below its long-run average of 54.66 since 2008.

Almost all of the improvement came from the forward-looking side of the survey.

"The improvement was driven largely by brighter expectations: that sub-index climbed to 48.41 from 44.82. Pocketbook confidence, covering personal finances and job security, was broadly unchanged at 54.94," said Nik Nanos, chief data scientist at Nanos Research.

"Even so, overall confidence remains below its long-run average of 54.66, suggesting Canadians are feeling somewhat better, but remain cautious about the economic outlook as the year moves ahead."

What do Canadians expect from home prices?

The Expectations Index combines views on the economy with views on neighbourhood real estate, and the housing component remains soft.

Just 29.10% of respondents expect local home values to rise over the next six months. That is below the 2026 average of 34.28% and the long-run average of 39.76%.

Another 45.65% expect prices to hold, while 19.96% anticipate a decline.

Household finances offer little cushion. Only 11.03% said their personal finances improved over the past year, compared with 37.91% who said they were worse off.

British Columbia was the only region in net-negative territory, at 46.02. Ontario sat just under neutral at 49.91.

A new international research by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) revealed that Canada’s inflation-adjusted home prices more than doubled between 2005 and 2025, rising 101% and outpacing every major peer country.

Fausto Gaudio of IC Savings argues that home prices remain too disconnected from incomes, making it increasingly difficult for first-time buyers to enter the market and highlighting the need for a broader affordability reset. https://t.co/3PehdHgrJn — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 13, 2026

How the confidence data fits the Bank of Canada rate call

Nanos said the Expectations Index has tracked year-over-year GDP growth with a 0.82 correlation on a six-month lag, and that the data has been cited in the Bank of Canada’s Monetary Policy Report. That makes the reading a timely input one week before the central bank’s October 28 decision. The overnight rate has stood at 2.25% since October 2025.

Most of the bank economists calling for an October 28 rate hold point to September’s inflation data.

Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres Group, addressed those figures amid rising business inflation expectations in the Bank’s latest survey.

“The September data support our base-case scenario that the Bank of Canada will remain on hold at its October 28 meeting,” she said.

Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada in Montréal, has urged brokers to recommend the five-year fixed over variable. He was direct about the risk of tightening. 

“I don’t think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking next week, and if they do hike, they can’t be too aggressive,” he noted.

items.title: Feeling Creative? Good Bones Hit The Trinity Bellwoods Market
items.description:
Our typical listing spotlight features the standard bells and whistles, including savvy staging. But sometimes, all it takes to make the eyes (and heart) linger is a bare-bones set of photos and a strong foundation.

This is the case with 13 Euclid Avenue. Tucked north of Queen, just around the corner from Trinity Bellwoods Park, this duplex — asking $999,700 — hits the market with its upper levels presenting as a clean state. With no staging, renderings, or AI imaginings (phew), the home can’t hide.

But with quality craftsmanship, that's not a problem.

Across 2.5 storeys, multiple elements feel (and may just be) straight from a past era. On arrival, you’re met by original hardwood flooring, which continues to make appearances across other areas of the home (including the top-floor bedroom — more on that shortly).

Original millwork, detailed plaster ceilings that soar to generous heights, and large windows that fill the space with natural light all bring a special type of character that’s difficult to emulate in a new build.

  • SPECS

    • Address: 13 Euclid Avenue, Toronto
    • Bedrooms: 4
    • Bathrooms: 2
    • Size: 1,500-2,000 sq. ft
    • Listed At: $999,700

The address is a working duplex; the lower unit — complete with its own kitchen and walkout to the backyard — is home to a tenant who, according to the listing, is happy to stay in place.

Make no mistake: there’s room for renovation and upgrades here, too. Whether it’s transforming the upper kitchen into an eat-in paradise, or combining landscaping with outdoor furniture to create a private backyard sanctuary, your imagination is the limit. But please, buyer-to-be — leave the blue bathroom tile intact.

______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

Our Favourite Thing

We've already given the bathroom tile its flowers, so here we'll celebrate the main top-level bedroom. Spanning some half of the home's top floor, this room features hardwood planks that are wider than elsewhere in the home — and we're swooning over them. Pair that floor with the uniquely angular ceiling, a skylight, and the quirky shelf built into the wall, and you have the perfect place to design a primary-bedroom sanctuary. That, or a reading nook for the ages.

______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

This address also comes complete with a detached garage off the laneway, a rare find for the area.

And speaking of the neighbourhood: beyond the craftsmanship, a key part of this home’s charm is its location — literal steps from the Queen West strip, calling 13 Euclid home would mean coffee at White Squirrel followed by a walk in the park as a daily routine. Sud Forno sandwiches would probably beckon most days, too. But we wouldn’t mind.

items.description: Standing inventory fell 7% from Q2, the first quarterly decline in four years, but it remains 40% higher than a year ago
items.content: <p>Standing inventory fell 7% from Q2, the first quarterly decline in four years, but it remains 40% higher than a year ago</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639281884371480188.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Standing inventory fell 7% from Q2, the first quarterly decline in four years, but it remains 40% higher than a year ago
items.body:
Investment groups are buying new condos in the Greater Toronto Hamilton Area at a time when end users largely aren’t. That demand pushed new condo apartment sales to 760 units in the third quarter, twice the total from a year earlier, according to Urbanation Inc.’s Q3-2026 Condominium Market Survey.

It was the second straight quarterly gain. In Q2, Urbanation’s second-quarter survey flagged HST relief and bulk buying as the drivers of the turn.

Over the past two quarters, 1,531 units have sold, close to the 1,578 units sold in all of 2025. Q3 activity was still 78% below the 10-year average for third quarters.

Bulk deals accounted for 339 units, or 45% of the quarter’s sales. They closed at an average of $763 psf, about 40% below the original selling prices in the same buildings.

Completed buildings produced a record 648 sales, an 85% share. Standing inventory fell 7% from Q2 to 5,127 units, the first quarterly decline in four years, but it remains 40% higher than a year ago.

Dan Eisner, founder and CEO of True North Mortgage, told Canadian Mortgage Professional earlier this year that investors would signal the Toronto condo market’s bottom. 

"If you can find a quality condo which is 750 square feet-plus, then you’re probably good. That’s where investors are going to move first – into those markets where [condos] are livable and the layout makes sense," he said. 

"If you see those properties starting to get picked up, then you know that you’re getting close to the bottom because that’s where the investors will come first."

Presales stay frozen

Pre-construction sales fell 61% from a year earlier to 60 units. Ontario’s enhanced HST rebate requires units bought as rentals to be substantially completed by Dec. 31, 2029. Most high-rise projects take four to five years to build, so they cannot meet that deadline.

At MortgageFest Canada, Christine Xu, founder of Money Broker Canada, described what has happened to presale investors. 

“Big shot realtors who bought so many pre-construction condos and now — bankruptcy. We see bankruptcy all over the place,” she said.

She also sees an opening: “For people who actually need to buy real estate for their own use, I think that’s really the best time to get into the market.”

Daniel Grechi, partner at Grechi Carter Real Estate Lawyers, said the distress is showing up in his firm’s work. 

“For us, the really interesting thing has been how the enforcement side of things is growing — with the way the market’s been, there’s a real need for that,” he noted.

Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada, says Ottawa should allow foreign buyers to purchase new-build homes, pointing to unsold condo inventory and the government's goal of making Canada more attractive to investors. https://t.co/hUVWtFthRu — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 20, 2026

A thinning pipeline

Construction starts totalled 381 units in Q3. Year-to-date starts are 82% below the 10-year average. Units under construction fell 38% to 35,920, the lowest level since early 2012, and scheduled completions drop to 4,213 units in 2029.

Shaun Hildebrand, president of Urbanation, warned that “with the pre-construction market remaining dormant and construction starts at historic lows, the supply pipeline is drying up, setting the market up for a significant shortage by the end of the decade.”

Eisner has made the same argument by warning that, “As no new condos are being built, that spells almost certain disaster for condo pricing.”

Once today’s inventory is absorbed, he said, buyers could face sharply higher prices.

Moves such as Jesta Group’s $500m bet on unsold Toronto inventory show where capital is going for now.

items.title: Empty homes tax debate swirls 10 years after pioneering tax in Vancouver
items.description: Developers warn the empty homes tax could increase costs and undermine new construction
items._ogDesc: Developers warn the empty homes tax could increase costs and undermine new construction
items.body:
The City of Vancouver launched a tax on empty dwellings 10 years ago that it billed as the first municipal tax of its kind anywhere in North America.

Debate swirls around how effective taxing empty homes is in helping the long-term housing market. This is despite even critics accepting that these taxes can help reduce the number of empty dwellings.

Since Vancouver introduced that initial empty homes tax, the concept has proved popular in public polling and among left-of-centre politicians that created similar themed taxes at the provincial and federal levels.

Governments roll out empty homes taxes over past decade

Gregor Robertson was Vancouver's mayor when he and his Vision Vancouver council approved the city's Empty Homes Tax (EHT) in November 2016. This came into effect Jan. 1, 2017.

Vancouver homeowners must submit an annual declaration so the city can determine whether their property is subject to the EHT.

Properties deemed or declared empty in 2025, for example, are subject to a three per cent tax on the property’s 2025 assessed value.

Former premier John Horgan and his NDP government were next to launch a tax on those who own vacant dwellings.

Enacted in 2018, the province's Speculation and Vacancy Tax (SVT) had its first declaration period for property owners in January and February 2019.

The SVT applies to municipalities across Metro Vancouver, the Capital Regional District in Greater Victoria and 26 other municipalities.

The province slaps a one per cent annual tax on Canadian citizens and permanent residents who own homes they leave vacant, while foreign residents who do that get a bigger tax bill, equal to three per cent of their property's assessed taxable value.

Former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau's government introduced its Underused Housing Tax (UHT) to take effect in January 2022.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government then earlier this year cancelled the UHT, saying the tax was costly and inefficient to administer, generating excessive compliance burdens and red tape for taxpayers.

Politicians promise new taxes on empty dwellings

Recent provincial and municipal election campaigns have provided further evidence of the popularity of the empty homes tax, particularly among left-of-centre politicians.

Former NDP MLA and Imagine Surrey leader Mike Starchuk, for example, promised during his recent mayoral campaign he would call on the provincial government to amend its Local Government Act to allow the City of Surrey create its own empty homes tax.

Vancouver was legally able to launch its pioneering EHT because it is governed by the Vancouver charter, which allows special taxing powers.

In contrast, the Local Government Act and Community Charter, which govern Surrey and other cities across the province, do not allow the same taxing powers.

Starchuk said he would apply his proposed municipal empty homes tax on dwellings left vacant for much of the year.

His intent is to reduce the asking price for new rents and help people find homes.

Starchuk said the initiative would also generate revenue to help fund affordable housing projects.

He is not alone in wanting to use taxation to help free up potential homes.

B.C. Premier David Eby, as NDP leader during the current election campaign, promised two separate measures to tax empty homes.

First, he pledged to introduce a new tax on condominiums that developers have completed but not sold.

This new condo tax would apply to finished units that have been left empty for more than a year and start at a two per cent rate.

The tax rate would then rise by one percentage point for each additional year that the units remain unsold and unoccupied, Eby said.

Eby explained the proposal in part by pointing to a Real Property Data report showing developers are sitting on about $4.4 billion worth of completed but empty homes.

Eby separately promised to increase the SVT’s rates to two per cent for domestic owners and to five per cent for foreign owners.

Number of empty homes fall in Vancouver after tax introduced

Reaction to the general concept of empty homes tax is mixed. Supporters point out evidence that the tax reduces the number of vacant homes. Others warn of unintended consequences and potential long-term harm to the housing market and economy.

Geoff Meggs, a Vision Vancouver councillor in the mid-2010s, told Business in Vancouver that he originally opposed the idea of bringing in an empty homes tax in Vancouver.

Vision Vancouver pushed for an empty homes tax while he was in office.

"I had reservations because it was not clear to me how big a problem it actually was," Meggs said.

Urban planning consultant Andy Yan had conducted a study of empty condominiums that used various data, including electricity consumption, to determine that Vancouver had a substantial number of vacant units.

Yan told BIV that his research focused on specific neighbourhoods in downtown Vancouver.

"The public was concerned because there were not enough lights on," Meggs said.

"But I wasn't sure how you could be sure that a place was empty, and therefore taxable. And how would you enforce it? I had all these questions, but we decided to do it because there was a lot of public concern."

He said his reticence turned out to be unfounded.

"The city was able to set up a system where people were required to disclose," he said. "It was quite simple. People had thought it would take forms that would go on forever, but it was a very straightforward online process that people declared and then people had to pay the tax."

Since the city implemented the tax, its data has shown a steady decline in the percentage of vacant homes in the city.

The city's annual report on the tax released last year showed, based on homeowner declarations, just 0.49 per cent of the homes in Vancouver are vacant—the lowest percentage since the tax launched.

That figure excludes vacant homes exempt from the tax because of fire damage, a court order restricting their use, a recent death or other reasons that the city considers valid.

The city's vacant home rate was 1.17 per cent in 2017, and in each successive year showed a decline.

In total, the number of vacant and exempted homes in Vancouver in 2024 was 4,697, or about 2.3 per cent of the city’s 201,739 total homes.

Of the other homes, 136,211 are principal residences and 60,831 are tenanted, according to the city.

Yan said he believes targeted taxes are effective at reducing the number of empty homes.

He pointed to a 2022 report by UBC economists Tsur Somerville and Jake Wetzel that found B.C.'s SVT has also been successful, returning approximately 20,000 vacant housing units to the long-term rental market in Metro Vancouver.

Taxes come with unintended consequences

Developers say taxes on vacant homes or on unsold inventory are misguided because they increase the cost of future development and can make projects financially unviable.

When developers get financing, they document their costs and risks and bring that to bankers, explained Michael Geller, a principal at Michael Geller Associates Ltd. and a longtime developer of small projects.

Higher costs and the risk of future taxes can force developers to take out larger loans and, in some cases, borrow at higher interest rates, he said.

One of Geller's main objections is that Vancouver's EHT is charged not only on empty homes, but also on empty development sites.

The city's rationale is that homeowners should not be able to avoid the tax by demolishing their dwellings, he explained.

The problem is that a development site can remain untouched because it is not financially viable for the owner to build homes and sell them at prices that cover costs and generate a profit, Geller said.

"The developer's permits may be held up," he added. "Maybe he can't arrange financing because there is no market. Meanwhile, in addition to his property taxes, he's now paying this empty homes tax that, one day, he'll have to try to recover from developing homes."

Geller also opposes Eby's promise to tax developers' unsold inventory of homes that have been vacant for more than a year.

Eby said at a news conference that B.C. needs this tax because developers are "hoarding" those units, waiting for them to go up in price.

"Nothing could be further from the truth," Geller told BIV. "The notion that they're hoarding them and keeping them off the market to maybe make them more valuable is preposterous."

The reality, he explained, is that lenders restrict developers' ability to sell the units.

Bankers almost always have clauses in lending agreements that set minimum prices at which developers are allowed to can sell units, he said.

If a developer sells a unit for below that set price, then the banker would require the developer to put in more capital of his or her own, Geller said.

He said bankers put these kinds of clauses in projects he developed, such as:

  • the four-unit Vinson House in West Vancouver;
  • the four-unit Ambleside Mews in West Vancouver; and
  • the 36-unit Elm Park Place in Vancouver.

Other developers stressed that developers are selling units as fast as they can.

Polygon Homes chairman Michael Audain told BIV that taxing empty homes or unsold condos is the "craziest idea I've ever heard."

He stressed that every completed condo that his company builds, it tries to sell as soon as it can. 

"We're not selling, certainly, at the rate that we were a few years ago, but we're selling everywhere at whatever the market will allow us to do because that's our business—to build and sell homes," he said. 

"There's no point putting a hammer on the developer to sell. The absorption can only be at a certain level, and demand is very low at the moment. You can't dump all your homes on the market at once."

Other developers told BIV that taxing developers for unsold inventory makes future development more costly, if not impossible.

"If the government is at all interested in encouraging housing development, this basically just shuts it down," Cressey Development Group executive vice-president Hani Lammam told BIV.

He said Cressey has no unsold inventory, although that could change this spring.

That is when Cressey expects to complete its 59-unit Rockford condominium project in Surrey, where 43 units were pre-sold.

Lammam said governments brought in empty homes taxes partly in response to the perception that wealthy foreign buyers owned B.C. homes as secondary residences.

"Circumstances have changed," Lammam said.

"There are no investors, virtually whatsoever, in the marketplace. The cost to produce the housing, when you aggregate all costs, is unaffordable for local incomes. So, the whole model is broken. Costs have to come down, or incomes have to go up."

Cressey has shifted over the past decade toward building more rental buildings and fewer condominium developments.

A tax on unsold inventory might push other developers to similarly shift toward building rental homes, Lammam said.

But he cautioned that building rental housing today is also challenging.

"Building rental was viable," he said. "Is it viable today, and are we starting new rental projects today? No, we're not because the costs are high and revenues are weak, and there's a flood of inventory."

That oversupply includes projects by the Musqueam First Nation, which has been able to build using different development requirements because the projects are on Musqueam territory, he said.

The Musqueam First Nation has finished the first phase of its Sen̓áḵw project at the south end of the Burrard Bridge—a development that has far less parking than the City of Vancouver would otherwise require.

That first phase delivered 1,409 units across three towers. When complete, Sen̓áḵw is expected to be the largest rental project in Vancouver's history, with 11 residential towers delivering providing more than 6,000 purpose-built rental homes.

The Musqueam are also involved in East Wind near UBC which is expected to deliver 451 rental homes, including apartments and townhouses, by 2029.

The post Canada’s Borrowing 2.2x Deficit, Payments To Hit 1 in 7 Dollars of Revenue: PBO appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: The PBO projects Canada's federal borrowing will outpace deficits 2-to-1, with debt servicing costs exploding to consume 1 in 7 revenue dollars by 2030.
items.body:
Is it a bird? A plane? No, it’s… the size of Canada’s debt servicing costs. The Parliamentary Budget Officer’s (PBO) latest Economic and Fiscal Outlook projects Ottawa will accumulate $333 billion in deficit spending over 5 years. However, the Government of Canada (GoC) will need to borrow nearly three-quarters of a trillion dollars. Debt servicing is now the fastest-growing federal expense, projected to consume almost 1 in 7 dollars of revenue by 2030.

Federal Borrowing To Grow More Than 2x As Much As Deficits

Ottawa will accumulate $333.3 billion in cumulative deficits from 2026-27 through 2030-31. At the same time, the GoC will borrow an additional $732.9 billion, according to the PBO’s projections. That’s roughly 2.2 times as much borrowing than the projected deficit—or a deficit less than half the size of new borrowing. It depends on whether you’re a half-insolvent or half-solvent kind of person.

One of the reasons behind the gap is accounting methodology. Loans are both a liability and an asset; just think of it like a mortgage. One borrower’s liability of $100k is an asset of $100k to the lender. In this case, the gap is driven by Crown corporations and acquiring other assets. When the GoC borrows $1 billion and lends it to a Crown corporation, it owes investors $1 billion, but it’s also owed $1 billion. The loan doesn’t increase the deficit, just interest costs and any resulting losses.

It’s debatable whether it’s a good or bad decision, but the consequences are much clearer. “Most simply, cash outlays drive borrowing, which in turn increase market debt and public debt charges, independent of how they are recorded on an accrual basis,” warns the PBO.

The PBO’s calculations show a sharp impact on public finances in the coming years.

Canada To Spend Almost 1 In 7 Dollars of Revenue On Debt Payments

The PBO warns that debt charges are now the fastest-growing public expense. Annual public debt charges are projected to climb from $24.5 billion in 2021-22 to $59.3 billion in 2026-27. Their projections show it explodes to $83.0 billion in 2030-31, much faster than revenue. The PBO estimates debt repayment will consume 13.6% of revenue by 2030-31, up from 10.5% in 2025-26. Debt servicing is set to grow 29.5% faster than revenue, consuming almost 1 in 7 dollars collected.

Most are likely to assume this is due to higher interest rates, but that’s not what the numbers show. The PBO explains that this mainly reflects a larger stock of debt, not higher interest rates. That’s the fanciest way to say the captain of this ship didn’t realize they lost their anchor.

items.title: Bet on fixed, not variable, National Bank economist tells brokers
items.description: Marion says long-end rates are near their peak and the 5-year fixed still looks attractive
items.content: <p>Marion says long-end rates are near their peak and the 5-year fixed still looks attractive</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639281203142883871.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Marion says long-end rates are near their peak and the 5-year fixed still looks attractive
items.body:
With additional reporting by Fergal McAlinden

With the Bank of Canada’s October 28 rate decision, accompanied by a full Monetary Policy Report one week away, Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada in Montréal, has offered Canada’s mortgage brokers a direct piece of advice: recommend the five-year fixed.

Marion made the case at the Mortgage Professionals Canada conference in Calgary on Wednesday, telling an audience of brokers and lenders that the country’s long-end rate cycle is approaching its ceiling — and that borrowers drifting toward shorter-term options may be underestimating the structural forces keeping rates elevated.

“It seems like mortgage holders are betting the house on short-term rates,” he said.

“In my forecast, I’d say, well, consider the 5-year rate because, you know, I think it’s attractive given what’s happening in the economy.”

His view runs against the current of the market. Variable-rate insured mortgages are running at approximately 3.79%, below the best five-year fixed insured rate of approximately 4.04%. That spread has driven a modest recovery in variable demand, with the variable-rate share climbing to 26% of the market, the first increase in three years, per a Mortgage Professionals Canada consumer survey conducted in February.

The case for caution

Marion argued the spread is misleading in the current environment. Geopolitical disruption, rising global defence spending, and an AI-driven electricity build-out are all exerting sustained upward pressure on long-term bond yields.

The Bank of Canada itself noted at its September 2 hold that “long-term bond yields have moved up globally, including in Canada” and signalled it was “prepared to adjust monetary policy as needed,” language that put an October hike back on the table. 

Marion was direct about the Bank’s October 28 decision: “I don’t think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking next week, and if they do hike, they can’t be too aggressive.”

He added that he does not expect another 100 basis points of increase in mortgage rates, and that “most of the increase that we’ve seen in interest rates is behind us.”

Why the client conversation has changed

That reading reinforces what practitioners are already hearing. Leah Zlatkin, mortgage broker and LowestRates.ca expert, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in April that “most borrowers still prefer the certainty of fixed payments, especially after the sharp increases to variable rates during the Bank of Canada’s rate-hiking cycle in 2022 and 2023.”

The stakes are material. Mortgage delinquency balances rose 32% year-over-year nationally in the first quarter of 2026, and 52% in Ontario, according to Equifax Canada’s Q1 2026 Market Pulse report, a sign that renewal strain is already visible in the data.

With variable-rate market share climbing back to 26% even as delinquencies rise, broker demand and rate behaviour suggests the fixed-versus-variable conversation has rarely been more consequential.

items.title: Inflation return to 2% thrown into doubt, Bank of Canada survey shows
items.description: Tariff uncertainty and surging oil prices push business inflation expectations higher in Q3 2026
items.content: <p>Tariff uncertainty and surging oil prices push business inflation expectations higher in Q3 2026</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639281168037513479.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Tariff uncertainty and surging oil prices push business inflation expectations higher in Q3 2026
items.body:
Business sentiment in Canada improved in the third quarter of 2026, but the Bank of Canada’s Business Outlook Survey (BOS) carries a harder signal for mortgage brokers.

Nearly a quarter of surveyed firms, the largest share since the question was introduced, say they cannot estimate when inflation will return to the central bank’s 2% target.

‘Too hard to say’: the new refrain on inflation

The survey, conducted between August 6 and September 2, shows the share of firms planning for a recession fell from 17% to 6%, the lowest reading since 2023. But roughly three-quarters of those interviews took place before Canada-US trade talks collapsed on August 21. Results gathered after that date show a sharp deterioration.

Claire Fan, senior economist at Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) in Toronto, summarized the shift plainly.

“Firms’ one- to two-year-ahead inflation expectations declined between May and August as oil prices and trade uncertainty moderated, but resurged in September to near spring highs as those trends reversed,” she wrote.

RBC’s analysis of the survey data puts one-year-ahead business inflation expectations at 3.7% in September, with two-year expectations rising to 3.1%.

Fan flagged the cost pass-through trend as a separate concern.

“Concerningly, half of firms surveyed — more than last quarter — plan to pass on cost increases to customers,” she wrote, noting that improved demand conditions and firms’ desire to recover margins compressed by earlier cost rounds are also driving the shift.

Canada’s annual inflation rate climbed to 3.1% in September, up from 3.0% in August, according to Statistics Canada data released Monday — and economists say the reading gives the BoC little reason to lift its overnight rate at the October 28 meeting. https://t.co/JN1kELMQ9B — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 19, 2026

Rate decision in focus as brokers seek clarity

For brokers advising clients ahead of the BoC’s October 28 decision, the picture is uncommonly unsettled. The annual consumer price index (CPI) rose to 3.1% in September, above the prior month’s reading.

Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres Group (DLCG) in Canada, said the September reading keeps a hold in play.

“The September data support our base-case scenario that the Bank of Canada will remain on hold at its October 28 meeting,” she said.

“Policymakers will continue to closely monitor incoming inflation data and stand ready to tighten policy if price pressures broaden and become more persistent.”

Fan framed the broader dilemma in terms mortgage brokers will recognize. “We continue to see fragile economic recovery as the biggest counterweight to heightened inflation risks, and expect caution from the BoC, especially when rising bond yields are already tightening financial conditions and raising borrowing costs for businesses and households,” she wrote.

RBC’s base case calls for no rate hikes until 2027, but Fan acknowledged that “risks to our base case forecast of no rate hikes until 2027 are tilted toward earlier moves — including potentially as early as next week’s decision.”

items.title: BMO BrokerEdge names new VP for Ontario and Atlantic Canada
items.description: A two-decade broker channel veteran takes charge of two of the bank’s largest regional markets
items.content: <p>A two-decade broker channel veteran takes charge of two of the bank’s largest regional markets</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/ca/046/0299_637076106142381277.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A two-decade broker channel veteran takes charge of two of the bank’s largest regional markets
items.body:
BMO BrokerEdge has appointed Barbara Cook as regional vice-president for Ontario and Atlantic Canada. Cook, who previously served as the bank’s senior business development manager for Toronto West, takes charge of two of the country’s largest regional broker markets.

Cook fills a position created by the elevation of Paula Oliveira, who transitioned into a broader strategic mandate across BMO’s sales and broker program functions.

Career rooted in national broker networks

Before joining BMO BrokerEdge in April 2024, Cook spent more than four years at Mortgage Centre Canada as vice-president of franchise development and later vice-president of national sales.

Prior to that, at VERICO Canada, in her role as vice-president of national business development, she recruited more than 26 brokerage firms into the network in 2017 and a further 19 in 2018, contributing more than $2.5 billion in funded volume during her tenure.

When she spoke with CMP in a Women of Influence feature spotlighting BMO BrokerEdge’s leadership, Cook explained the thinking behind her move to the bank-owned channel:

“When I heard BMO was returning to the broker space, I thought what a great opportunity to make an impact on this side of the business, and I made the strategic move in April 2024.”

Her standing in the industry extends well beyond any single employer. Cook joined the board of Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) in October 2022 as an Ontario director, progressing through vice-chair and chair before completing her term as past chair in October 2026.

A pivotal moment for the broker channel

In announcing the appointment, Jamie Doolittle, head of BMO BrokerEdge in Canada, pointed to the breadth of Cook’s career.

“Throughout her career, she has built a strong reputation for driving business growth, developing high-performing teams, and fostering meaningful partnerships across the broker community,” Doolittle wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Cook was direct about what she intends to bring to the role.

“I’m excited to step into my new role with BMO BrokerEdge and continue championing the growth and success of our industry. I look forward to working alongside the incredible team across Ontario and Atlantic, supporting our brokers, strengthening relationships, and building on the momentum ahead,” she said.

A multiple recipient of the CMP Women of Influence recognition between 2018 and 2025 and winner of the Women of Distinction Award at the 2020 Canadian Mortgage Awards, Cook has also been a consistent public voice for gender equity and mentorship across the broker community.

items.title: Canada’s Approved-But-Unstarted Homes Climb As Starts Slide
items.description:
Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) counted 143,929 homes in September that have approved building permits and no construction started.

That count, reported alongside CMHC’s figures for centres of 50,000 or more, rose 1.1% from August.

Compared with a year ago, starts have fallen. Actual housing starts in centres of 10,000 or more were down 11% year-over-year in September, at 19,984 units compared with 22,375. From January through September, those centres recorded 170,964 starts, 4% behind the same period in 2025.

“As outlined in CMHC’s latest Housing Supply Report (HSR), a key risk for Canada now is not building enough during this period of softening housing markets across the country,” said Aled ab Iorwerth, deputy chief economist at CMHC.

“Canada still faces a long-term housing supply gap and unless housing construction levels increase, improvements in housing affordability since 2023 will be difficult to sustain,” he said.

Right now, starts are down from last year.

The headline figures make that harder to see: the seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) of starts across Canada rose 3% in September, to 248,896 units from 242,223 in August. CMHC’s six-month trend, a moving average of that rate, barely budged, and landed at 250,411.

CMHC uses the trend alongside the monthly SAAR to account for considerable swings in the monthly figure. Multi-unit starts largely drive the market, and they can vary widely from one month to the next.

Homes already underway are holding steady. There were 371,617 units under construction in centres of 50,000 or more in September, flat from August. Completions fell 0.9% to 17,398 units.

The regional picture is uneven. “Of Canada’s four most populous provinces, only Quebec has seen modest gains in housing starts for 2026 and each of the seven major centres covered in the HSR are behind 2025’s pace for new home construction,” ab Iorwerth said.

Montreal’s six-month trend fell 8% in September on lower multi-unit starts. Vancouver’s rose 6% on higher multi-unit starts. Toronto’s was flat, with single-detached and multi-unit trends offsetting each other.

CMHC will release October’s housing starts data on November 17.
